title: Small payload amplification in proxy chains — bench notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working note about an observed amplification of latency and system call overhead for very small payload RPCs when requests traverse multiple proxy hops (edge -> sidecar -> service). The hypothesis is that framing+serialization, TCP/TLS recordization, and per-hop buffering/flush policies combine to multiply the per-request overhead for sub-200B bodies.

Why we care:
- Many customer use-cases (assistant metadata, signal pings, ephemeral reranks) issue lots of tiny requests.
- Cost: amplified CPU/syscall + longer tails -> worse p99s and higher VM counts for same throughput.
- UX: interactive features seeing 5–20ms extra tail latency that is hard to attribute.

High-level findings (tl;dr):
- Direct client -> model-server baseline: single-digit ms median for 120B JSON request on our test hardware (see infra below).
- Add a single Envoy edge proxy (default config): +6–9ms median, +~12–20ms p99 depending on TLS and flush settings.
- Add a second hop (sidecar in the service pod): additional +3–8ms median, but p99s amplify nonlinearly.
- gRPC (protobuf) vs HTTP+JSON: protobuf reduces serialization bytes (~30–50%) and reduces amplification slightly — but framing and TLS recordization still dominate.
- Disabling Nagle (TCP_NODELAY) reduced median by ~1–2ms for sub-100B responses but increased CPU/syscall rate.

Experimental setup:
- HW: 4x m5a.large-ish instances for client/proxies/server (test cluster). 8 vCPU equivalent, 32GB RAM. Kernel 5.15.
- Server: minimal echo endpoint in our runtime that returns N bytes of payload. Builds: serving-runtime:v2026.11.21-bench
- Proxies tested: Envoy (v1.28, default), nginx (1.22), our internal edge-proxy (dev branch with batching on by default).
- Protocols: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 (gRPC), HTTP/2 with gRPC/protobuf vs HTTP/1.1+JSON.
- Payload sizes: 40B, 120B, 320B, 1KB. Focus on 40–320B.
- Concurrency: single connection 1–32 concurrent clients. Also measured high-concurrency batch.
- Load tools: wrk2 for HTTP, ghz for gRPC, custom python harness for controlled single-request latency.
- Instrumentation: eBPF (bcc) traces for syscalls (write/sendto), tcpdump to inspect TLS records, strace for syscall counts on server+proxy, and kernel TCP_CORK interactions.

Important low-level observations:
- TLS record size matters: for 120B JSON payload, with typical TLS overhead and HTTP headers the library emits multiple small TLS records (e.g., 1st record small header, 2nd record the payload). Each TLS record flush triggers a kernel send/write.
- Proxy buffering/flush policy: Envoy default behavior flushes per HTTP frame/buffer boundary; with small frames it emits multiple writes. Nginx has more aggressive coalescing in many configs. Our edge-proxy had a batching setting that attempted to aggregate many requests but added 2–6ms due to batching wait time — that tradeoff is visible.
- gRPC uses a 5-byte length-prefix per message; combined with HTTP/2 frame headers the per-message overhead is slightly smaller in bytes than JSON+headers but still suffers from recordization.
- System call and context-switch budget: per-request write+flush counts increase proportionally with hop count. For 40B payloads we counted ~6–9 write/send syscalls per hop (TLS+framing+headers), comparing direct vs 2-hop chain increased syscall rate dramatically.
- Nagle vs TCP_NODELAY: with Nagle enabled we saw higher latency due to TCP coalescing wait; disabling reduced latency at cost of more syscalls.

Representative numbers (median / p99 in ms) — 120B JSON request, TLS on, default Envoy: 
- client->server (direct): median 4.7 ms / p99 10.2 ms
- client->edge->server (edge=Envoy): median 11.0 ms / p99 28.3 ms
- client->edge->sidecar->server (Envoy+sidecar nginx): median 14.2 ms / p99 45.7 ms
- Same chain but protobuf/gRPC: median 9.0 ms / p99 21.4 ms

Per-hop syscall breakdown (approx, from strace):
- Client write (TLS): 2–3 writes per request
- Edge proxy: 6–9 writes/reads (parse headers, forward TLS record(s))
- Sidecar: 4–6 writes/reads
- Server: 2–3 writes to respond
Total observable writes: ~18–24 for 2-hop chain (small payloads)

What amplifies tail behavior:
- Small scheduler jitter: extra context switches at proxies add variable queuing before write/flush.
- TLS handshake reuse vs new sessions: keepalive is essential; new TLS handshakes kill everything.
- OS-level buffer limits and TCP_CORK interactions: some middleboxes/proxy code uses corking to coalesce but mis-tuned cork windows add tens of ms.
- Backpressure: when the server K/V cache warming or large token generation bursts happen, proxies buffer and then flush many records; small requests get delayed behind bursting flows.

Comparisons: serialization formats
- Raw JSON (120B) -> wire ~250–380 bytes after headers/TLS records in our traces
- protobuf payload (same semantic content) -> wire ~180–260 bytes
- msgpack is similar to protobuf in size, but our server libs had slightly higher CPU to encode/decode (not significant at these sizes).
Result: serialization choice helps but is second-order to TLS+frame overhead.

Actionable mitigations tested (and tradeoffs):
1) Enable write coalescing at first proxy (buffer up to 1ms or 512B): reduces syscalls and median by 4–6ms, but can add 1–3ms for latency-sensitive clients (tradeoff depends on workload).
2) Tune Envoy flush/beacon settings (stream idle timers, flush interval): small wins if tuned per-path; tricky to maintain globally.
3) Use HTTP/2 (gRPC) with single multiplexed connection per client: reduces handshake and header repetition. Improves p50/p90 but p99 still affected by proxy scheduling.
4) Use protobuf to shave wire bytes — helps x% for CPU and network but not a cure.
5) Bypass certain proxy hops for known low-risk, small RPCs (policy-level): biggest win operationally but introduces security/observability gaps.
6) Push batching to client (combine tiny requests) — often best for amortizing fixed cost but not always possible.
7) Evaluate TLS record coalescing in our TLS stack (OpenSSL settings): small wins with adjusted record_size_hint and writev usage.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How many real customer RPCs are in the <200B category? Need telemetry query (SR-4892) to quantify.
- Do our dedicated customers run sidecar chains that are avoidable by configuration? (CS outreach).
- Could we implement lightweight UDP-based control-plane for tiny pings (probably no).
- Is it worth building an opt-in low-latency path in our edge for sub-256B requests that bypass some processing (auth/observability) but leaves an immutable audit trail? Security review required.

Immediate next steps:
- Run broader sweep across regions and instance types (m5 vs c6i) to validate CPU contribution (assigned to Arjun, SR-4892).
- Add telemetry ping in production (sampled) for request sizes and number of proxy hops (Lucia).
- Prototype an Envoy config snippet with flush intervals and tcp_nodelay adjustments; measure at scale (Ryan).
- Draft a short one-pager for product describing options (security vs perf tradeoffs).

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Attach raw pcap traces and strace logs to the Jira ticket (do this before EOD Thu).
- Try disabling TLS at edge only (mTLS internal) to isolate TLS recordization cost.
- Consider adding eBPF histogram for sendmsg syscall latency per-process.

References and useful commands used:
- wrk2 -t1 -c1 -d30s --script=small-post.lua http://client/echo
- ghz --insecure --n=20000 --concurrency=1 --proto echo.proto --call Echo.Echo --data requests.json target:443
- sudo tcpdump -w small-120b-epoch.pcap -i eth0 port 443
- sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_sendto /comm=="envoy"/ { @[stack] = count(); }'
- strace -f -c -p <pid> (for per-process syscall counts)

Appendix: quick config snippets (Envoy) — rough
- stream_idle_timeout: 0s
- http1_protocol_options: { idle_timeout: 1s }
- typed_config for upstream: enable_reuse: true, flush_interval_ms: 1
(we need to push these to dev clusters carefully)

End of note.

If you picked this up: add any other places you recall tiny-RPC patterns (apps, eval pipelines) and we'll prioritize instrumentation.
